meta.title: Past editions — The Lord of the Rings: Battle for Middle-earth
meta.description: More than thirty years of battles for Middle-earth. The story of the event from the first edition in Rakovec Valley in 1992 to the current Křtiny era.

hero.subtitle: More than thirty years of battles for Middle-earth — from Rakovec Valley 1992 to today's strong wave.

intro.h2: Thirty years — chronicle of a community
paragraphs: The Lord of the Rings is not just a list of battles and dates in a calendar. It is the chronicle of a community that has repeatedly returned to Middle-earth since 1992, each time slightly differently and each time with a different generation of players, organisers and stories. The first edition in Rakovecké údolí had roughly 60 participants. Twelve years later, the event crossed the thousand-attendee mark, and in the modern wave it has stabilised at hundreds of people.

Over that time almost everything has changed: locations, organising teams, rules, event length, the emphasis on battle versus story, and participant expectations. But several things have stayed: Tolkien's world as the common language, woods and meadows as the playing space, volunteer work behind the scenes, and the appetite to meet around a story that's bigger than one weekend.

chapters.title: Attendance chart 1992–2025
chapters.body_html:
How to read the chart

This is not a simple popularity curve. Every major change in the graph has its context. The growth between 2001 and 2004 reflects a period of strong interest in fantasy and the chance to host the event with larger facilities. The decline after 2005 doesn't just mean lost interest — it also reflects venue changes, a new generation of organisers, and more demanding safety and organisational requirements.

The year 2014 must be read as a disrupted / cancelled edition, not as a normal turnout. And the years 2022–2025 show that, even after more than thirty years, The Lord of the Rings still has the power to draw large crowds — 2025 with 690 participants is the second-strongest recorded entry in the whole history of the event.

chapters.title: 1992–1997 — Beginnings in Rakovec Valley
chapters.body_html:
The first edition was held in 1992 in Rakovecké údolí. Surviving figures show 60 participants. In the early years it was mainly an adventure battle inspired by Tolkien, transferred into a real landscape. The scale was smaller, the rules simpler, and much of the magic rested on personal agreements, improvisation and enthusiasm.

The years 1993 to 1997 show a rapid search for form. The event kept returning to Rakovecké údolí, but Dobříš and Jelení louky also appeared. By 1997 the table already shows around 450 participants — the first really big jump. With this, The Lord of the Rings shifted from a smaller gathering into a notable fantasy battle.

The memoirist texts capture this period well. They are not dry records of winners and losers but pictures of a game where epic, chaos, humour, fatigue, rain, diplomacy and personal heroism all met. The early editions weren't just smaller — they were formative: in them the game's language, fighting style, sense of factions and the first memoirist legends took shape.

"About time you arrived — I've been waiting for you here."

— Aragorn's memoir, The Lord of the Rings 1992

chapters.title: 1998–2000 — Searching for venues and the split year 1999
chapters.body_html:
The late nineties are less clear, but precisely for that reason historically interesting. 1998 is linked to the Czech-Moravian Highlands. 1999 has two entries: edition 8A in Luteč between Brno and Vyškov and edition 8 in Vrané nad Vltavou. This shows that the tradition didn't evolve as a perfectly straight line. It was alive, branching in places, and dependent on the people who were willing and able to carry the event at that moment.

The year 2000 in Olešná near Havlíčkův Brod is then a return to greater continuity. The figure of 150 participants seems smaller compared with the later boom, but in the context of the Czech LARP scene at the time it was still a significant event.

chapters.title: 2001–2004 — The Špejchar era and major growth
chapters.body_html:
The year 2001 brings Křešice near Olbramovice and the place known as Špejchar. This was the era that became one of the most defining in the event's history. In 2001 the table shows 220 participants, in 2002 already 430, in 2003 around 680, and in 2004 the peak of 1100.

The Špejchar era combined a large player base, a strong story framework and the chance to run the game with bigger peoples, fortresses and wider terrain. At the same time it began to show clearly that a large fantasy battle isn't just weekend fun but an organisationally demanding project: transport, facilities, registration, safety, medics, communication with participants, rules and responsibility for hundreds of people.

The year 2003 is important in memoirist materials also story-wise. Surviving texts recall it as the edition when the game came strikingly close to the book story and when, after several years, the Ring was to be destroyed. That is exactly the kind of event you can't read out of a table, but which stays in the community's memory.

"Hi, we're the Eagles and Kukačka."

— The Eagles' view, 2003

chapters.title: 2005–2009 — Peak, relocation and generational handover
chapters.body_html:
The year 2004 is the first big peak — attendance crossed a thousand and The Lord of the Rings reached a scale that is remarkable even in retrospect. But such size also has its cost: more pressure on organisers, a greater need for clear rules, more demand on space, communication and safety.

After the peak came relocation and a gradual decline. The year 2005 took place at Tarn estate near Beroun and the table shows around 600 participants. From 2006 the event moves to Veverské Knínice. In this phase, alongside Jana "Jixipen" Syrovátková, Moravian LARP and a younger organising generation become ever more visible — from 2007 the records mention Michal "Mealtiner" Truhlář, from 2008 also "Glaren", and by 2009 Moravian LARP, o. s. is already listed as the main organising body.

The years 2006 to 2009 are not a weak phase but a phase of transition. After enormous numbers comes the search for sustainability. The event shrinks, transforms and again asks what a modern Lord of the Rings event should actually look like.

Public listings on LARP.cz: 2005 · 2006 · 2007 · 2008 · 2009

chapters.title: 2010–2011 — Return to Rakovec Valley and the twentieth edition
chapters.body_html:
The year 2010 brings a return to Rakovecké údolí near Bukovinka and around 350 attendees. The 2010 public listing describes the edition as a turning point — a new location and new rules, a life-points system in a revised version. The year 2011 is the twentieth edition and is shown in the table as roughly 400 estimated participants. From today's perspective it's a milestone: The Lord of the Rings no longer had to be the biggest at any cost. What mattered was that it still existed, had a team, and had a community that wanted to keep coming back.

This is exactly where the strength of tradition shows. The big battles in the Czech Republic gradually changed — some disappeared, others professionalised or shrank. But The Lord of the Rings survived thanks to a combination of memory, personal ties and willingness to repeatedly put in a great deal of invisible organisational work.

Public listings on LARP.cz: 2010 · 2011

chapters.title: 2012–2015 — Restart under the name Battle for Middle-earth
chapters.body_html:
From 2012 the name The Lord of the Rings – Battle for Middle-earth appears more often. Internal and public sources sometimes diverge here, so for these years it pays to distinguish registrations, publicly stated capacity and real attendance.

2012 has 454 in the internal data, 2013 has 356. The year 2014 is unusual and needs to be read carefully: the internal table shows 164 registrations together with a note that the event was cancelled because of the weather. 2015 then sits at around 95 internally recorded participants.

From the outside it looks like a slump, but historically it's rather a restart point. The event shrank but didn't disappear. From a smaller, more sustainable form it later began to grow again.

Public listings on LARP.cz: 2012 · 2013 · 2014 · 2015

chapters.title: 2016–2021 — Recovery and new organising generation
chapters.body_html:
The years 2016–2021 are a recovery phase. After the smaller restart, the numbers gradually rise: 178 in 2016, 197 in 2017, 258 in 2018, 211 in 2019, 289 in 2020 and 475 in 2021. These figures show that trust, rhythm and organisational continuity were rebuilt.

At the same time the team is changing. Alongside Mealtiner, the available records also mention other organisers and co-organisers — Radis, Monty, Inzzi, Kristy, Špajda, Ozzyáš and others. This is essential for the history: The Lord of the Rings has never been just one person or one table. It has been a repeatedly renewed team project.

The years 2020 and 2021 also took place in the shadow of the pandemic situation. The LARP.cz public listing showed the date 27–30 August 2021 near Křtiny with a note on the situation at the time. And yet it is precisely after this period that the strong current wave begins to rise again.

Public listings on LARP.cz: 2016 · 2017 · 2018 · 2019 · 2020 · 2021

chapters.title: 2022–2025 — Today's strong wave
chapters.body_html:
The years 2022 to 2025 show The Lord of the Rings as a living and growing event again. Final internal numbers report 570 participants in 2022, 523 in 2023, 513 in 2024 and 690 in 2025. According to the unified chart, 2025 is therefore the second-strongest recorded entry after the 2004 peak.

Geographically the event mainly sticks to Křtiny and its surroundings (the meadow between Křtiny and Bukovina, the meadow above the town). The 2024 edition ultimately took place at Rozkoš near Znojmo — thus outside the established Křtiny camping ground. For 2026 the tradition returns to Křtiny / Bukovina.

The current era is important because it doesn't work just as nostalgia for veterans. New players, families, younger participants arrive — as do people who know The Lord of the Rings rather as an open fantasy battle than as a historical LARP institution. With this, the tradition rewrites itself again: the old story gets a new audience.

Public listings on LARP.cz: 2022 · 2023 · 2024 · 2025

chapters.title: Myths and editorial notes
chapters.body_html:
"The Lord of the Rings has always had one fixed form."

He hasn't. In different years the length, locations, rules, narrative emphasis and size all changed. It is precisely this variability that is one of the reasons the event has survived for so long.

"The decline after 2004 meant the end of interest."

Not so simply. After the record edition came a venue change, organisational complexity, generational shift, and the search for a sustainable size. The graph shows a decline, but the history shows more of a transition and later renewal.

"2014 is an ordinary edition with low attendance."

No. In the internal data, the year 2014 carries a note about cancellation due to weather. It is therefore appropriate to keep it in the graph and table, but explain it in the text as a disrupted edition.

"The current editions are just a nostalgic return."

Current data doesn't support that. The years 2022–2025 show stable high attendance, and 2025 ranks among the strongest recorded entries ever.

chapters.title: Closing — chronicle of a community
chapters.body_html:
The Lord of the Rings is the chronicle of a community. It started as an adventure battle inspired by Tolkien, grew into a thousand-strong event, went through decline, handovers and a restart, and in recent years it's growing strong again. It isn't a perfectly polished story. There is chaos, enthusiasm, weather, venue moves, mismatched tables, memoirist legends and a lot of work you don't see on the photos.

And precisely for that reason it is worth telling. Not as a museum exhibit, but as a living tradition that, for more than three decades now, keeps returning to one simple question: who will rise this year to defend Middle-earth?

chapters.title: Venues — where the battles for Middle-earth have been fought
chapters.body_html:
Over three decades, The Lord of the Rings has travelled much of the Czech LARP map. It began in Rakovecké údolí, then moved to Dobříš, Jelení louky, the Czech-Moravian Highlands, Luteč, Vrané nad Vltavou, Olešná and Křešice near Olbramovice. Špejchar near Křešice became one of the most important sites in the whole history, because that was where the event grew into hundreds of participants and reached its largest scale.

After 2005 came Beroun and Veverské Knínice. Newer editions are publicly associated mainly with Křtiny and the area between Křtiny and Bukovina. The 2024 edition made a one-off move to Rozkoš near Znojmo; for 2026 the tradition returns to Křtiny.

chapters.title: Archival snippets — quotes and memories
chapters.body_html:
From surviving reports and memoirist texts we pick out short excerpts that show well how the game was experienced. The full texts deserve a separate archival publication after copy-editing.

"About time you arrived — I've been waiting for you here."

— Aragorn's memoir, The Lord of the Rings 1992. An opening atmospheric touch of old stylisation and humour.

"Five scouts moved through very tall grass. They carried only their weapons and nerves stretched to the breaking point."

— Petr Suchánek, battle report 1995. A sample of the early report style — battle chronicle, in-game narration and personal irony.

Lords of the Horses against the Lord of the Rings

— Report 2002. A view from the Rohan riders and a literary reconstruction of troop movements, fortress falls, retreats and last desperate attempts.

"Hi, we're the Eagles and Kukačka."

— The Eagles' view, 2003. Period humour and memoirist exaggeration — a sample of how legends also give birth to jokes.

"Organising events for others, seeing them enjoy the game, singing with them around the fires, later hearing back their memories and impressions — it's simply worth it."

— a memoir piece for the twentieth anniversary of The Lord of the Rings.

chapters.title: Sources and notes on credibility
chapters.body_html:
The basic backbone for 1992–2011 is formed by attached historical tables and memoirist documents (including Twenty Years of The Lord of the Rings). The data supplement from 2012 onwards uses an internal workbook and public research via LARP.cz and the LARP Database.

footer_alert.body_html: We collect materials about individual editions. If you have photos, reports or memories that would fit the archive, write to us at info@panprstenu.cz. Meanwhile you can find more material in the Gallery and in News.
